reason: A specification whose only event never changes state -- a null detector. Design D-7 measured this hit on the frozen control and noted it would have no successor because SecretKeySpec.mop was to be deleted; D-11 withdrew that deletion and keeps all 23 files, so the hit survives with the file. It accuses nothing (no state change, no report site of its own), so leaving it costs no accusation; deleting the specification would be a change of the set's membership and belongs to whoever revisits D-11.

G-2b' flags an event whose out-alphabet at the unsafe state is a subset of the safe state's -- the idiom every `g3`/`g4`-style unsafe-getInstance event of this set uses on purpose: it records the algorithm without changing state, so the accusation lands on the call that consumes it. Design D-7 measured exactly these eight on the frozen control (CipherSpec.g3, KeyGeneratorSpec.g3, KeyManagerFactorySpec.g3, KeyPairGeneratorSpec.g3, KeyStoreSpec.g2, MacSpec.g3, MessageDigestSpec.g4, SecretKeySpec.e1) and states why the gate is a question rather than a verdict: its implied repair is absorption, which gh101 D-S9 rejected as trading a false positive for a false negative. One row for all eight, because the reason is one reason; the set is unchanged from the frozen baseline.

A redundant state in the specification D-7 already names as the set's null detector. It accuses nothing and is the same artefact as the G-2a row above, seen from the state side; it survives for the same reason (D-11 keeps the file).

The gate reads `sink = highest index` as a violation state; SecretKeySpec declares no `fail` category, so its highest-index state is not a violation state and the reading does not apply. Measured as such on the frozen control by D-7. The file survives under D-11.

Same as the SecretKeySpec row: RandomStringPasswordSpec has no `fail` category, so `sink = highest index` names no violation state. D-7 measured both; both files survive under D-11, which is why the two hits have successors where D-7 expected none.

IvChainJunction.mop is a predicate-only consumer specification: it exists so that api30 Cipher's guarded `preparedIV[params]` clause (Cipher.cryptsl:182) has a site that binds the third argument of `init`, which `CipherSpec.i2` does not and `CipherSpec` cannot gain an event for at 17 of 17 (INV-INS-145). It states no ORDER of its own -- the ordering of Cipher is CipherSpec's -- so `ere : use*` accepts every sequence and the accusation lives in the event body, where `params` is in scope. This is the event side: the transition row is the identity ([0, 1]) because the automaton is not what accuses. Same shape as the SecretKeySpec.e1 row above, with one difference worth naming -- that one is a legacy artefact the set tolerates until whoever revisits D-11, this one is the design, and a transition row that stopped being the identity here would mean a typestate claim had been added by accident.

G-ORDER reports `c1 r1 c` accepted by the api30 ORDER and rejected by the specification. The excess is on the rule's side and has no repair here: the rule's `c1` is CipherInputStream's one-argument constructor, which android-30 declares `protected`. No application site can reach it and the pointcut asks for `public`, correctly, so the rule orders an event no monitored program produces. Closing this would need a disposition on the rule side of `order_alphabet_map.csv`, which the format does not have -- `order-unmapped` erases an event of the `.mop`, never a symbol of the rule. Measured in the mapping pass that first made the divergence sayable; the fourteen specifications skipped `for want of rows` had been hiding it.

G-ORDER reports `c2 c` accepted by the specification and rejected by the api30 ORDER. The rule places `fl` (`flush()`) inside a mandatory repetition group, so a stream that only flushes and closes is refused by the rule and accepted by the `ere`. The rule declares `flush` nowhere else, and the exemption did not manufacture the divergence -- it revealed it. Repairing it would tighten what the specification accuses, which is a behavioural change this change's decision 7 keeps out without a measurement of its own.

G-ORDER reports `g1 i1 u1` accepted by the specification and rejected by the api30 ORDER: the `ere` accepts an unfinalised Cipher. The witness exists only because task 7.1 repaired the gate's precedence parser -- `CrySL.xtext:103-120` binds `,` weaker than `|`, and `Cipher` is the one api30 rule whose language the two parses tell apart. It is a genuine slack of the specification, and closing it is a behavioural change: it would make the monitor accuse a program that updates and never finalises, which nothing in the corpus does today. Recorded in `data/gh105/evidence/f1-order-gate-precedence.md`.

G-ORDER reports `g1 g1 gk` accepted by the specification and rejected by the api30 ORDER: a benign slack of the `g1+`/`g2+` repetition. The specification is inherited unchanged from the frozen `jca` set, whose measurements are published and whose files task 8.2 has to prove untouched. Repairing it here would edit a divergence that belongs to the frozen control, not to this change.

G-ORDER reports the empty sequence accepted by the api30 ORDER and rejected by the specification: the rule's `co?` is optional and the `ere` requires the constructor, so a KeyPair that came out of `generateKeyPair()` and is then asked for `getPublic()` is accused. The specification's own comments already measured this and deferred it to task 7.1. Loosening the `ere` is a behavioural change -- it would silence the accusation for every KeyPair the program did not construct itself -- and needs its own corpus measurement.

G-ORDER reports `g2 l1` accepted by the api30 ORDER and rejected by the specification, and this one accuses a conforming program: the `.mop` declares no event for `getInstance(String, String)`, because its `g1` and `g2` both match the same one-argument overload under a negated guard. A program that uses the provider overload is unobserved at `getInstance`, so its `load` falls into `@fail`. The specification is inherited from the frozen `jca` set; adding the overload is a change of the set's alphabet and belongs to whoever revisits the freeze.

G-ORDER reports `g1 Init se1 se1` accepted by the specification and rejected by the api30 ORDER: the `end` state admits a second `engine` against the rule's `Gets, Init, Engine?`. The specification's own comment at `SSLContextSpec.mop:186-189` records the slack. It is the same shape as the KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory pair task 7.1 repaired, but the opposite direction -- there the specification was too strict and the repair silenced nothing; here it is too permissive and a repair would start accusing a second `createSSLEngine()`, which is a behavioural change with no measurement yet.

G-ORDER reports `d` accepted by the api30 ORDER and rejected by the specification. The excess is on the rule's side: `d` is `destroy()`, which the `.mop` deliberately does not observe because it throws `DestroyFailedException` in both implementations this set sees, so an `after returning` advice would have no execution path (INV-INS-137). As with CipherInputStreamSpec, the mapping format has no disposition for a symbol of the rule -- `order-unmapped` erases an event of the `.mop` -- so the row is the only place this decision can be written down.

G-ORDER reports `c1 c1` accepted by the specification and rejected by the api30 ORDER: a self-loop of `init` over the constructor, which the rule's `Ins` does not repeat. The specification's comment at `SecureRandomSpec.mop:253-262` records it, and `data/gh105/evidence/f2-SecureRandomSpec.md` carries the measurement. Removing the self-loop would accuse a program that constructs a SecureRandom twice on one binding, which is a behavioural change of its own.
